description:
A generated meta-voice grammar aggregating every interpretation grammar in this repo into one navigable set: one item per planet, sign, and house, each carrying every voice's own reading of that placement side by side — Ptolemy, Lilly, Jyotiṣa, Alan Leo, the planetary myths, and the platform's own Canonical synthesis. Cast a placement and hear every tradition answer at once.

SOURCE OF TRUTH — read this first. Each voice's authoritative interpretation lives in its own grammar at `grammars/<slug>/grammar.json`. This meta is a *generated index* (a projection) over those voices, rebuilt idempotently by `scripts/build_meta_astro.py` — it is NOT a second copy to maintain. To correct an entry, edit its source voice; the meta re-derives. Coverage varies by entity — a voice with no historical entry for a given placement (e.g. Lilly only wrote on the seven planets, not signs or houses) simply has no section there; nothing is invented to fill a gap. See docs/DESIGN-oracle-trinity.md ('Astro of all Astros') for the design this proves out.

sections.Canonical:
**Story:** The Sun is your core identity — who you are becoming. It represents your conscious will, creative force, and the central organizing principle of your life.

**Light:** Vitality, self-expression, leadership, creative power, confidence, generosity.

**Shadow:** Ego inflation, domination, burnout from over-identification with achievement.

**Archetype:** The King/Queen — sovereign consciousness that gives light and warmth.
sections.Ptolemy (Tetrabiblos):
**Interpretation:** The Sun is found to produce heat and moderate dryness. His magnitude, and the changes which he so evidently makes in the seasons, render his power more plainly perceptible than that of the other heavenly bodies; since his approach to the zenith of any part of the earth creates a greater degree of heat in that part.

**Light:** The Sun and Mercury are deemed of common influence, and productive either of good or evil in unison with whatever planets they may be connected with. The Sun is diurnal and masculine.

**Shadow:** When afflicted, the Sun's heating influence may become excessive, creating imbalance in the constitution.

**The record — Ptolemy, tr. Ashmand (1822):** *Book I, Ch. IV–VII, on the Sun's temperament and sect (excerpted, fetched from sacred-texts.com; … marks elisions):*

> The Sun is found to produce heat and moderate dryness. His magnitude, and the changes which he so evidently makes in the seasons, render his power more plainly perceptible than that of the other heavenly bodies; since his approach to the zenith of any part of the earth creates a greater degree of heat in that part and proportionately disposes its inhabitants after his own nature. … The Sun and Mercury are deemed of common influence, and productive either of good or evil in unison with whatever planets they may be connected with. … The Sun, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are called masculine. … The day, in its heat and its aptitude for action, is masculine … the Sun and Jupiter, diurnal.
sections.Lilly (1647):
**What Lilly reads:** The Sun's significations here are an unbroken ladder of rank — king down through every grade of gentleman and courtier — with no separate psychological or emotional register at all. In this text the Sun IS social position; nothing about 'identity' or 'ego' in the modern sense the tropical-canonical library uses (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical).

**Lilly's own words:** "He signifies kings, princes, emperors, &c.; dukes, marquisses, earls, barons, lieutenants, deputy lieutenants of counties, magistrates, gentlemen in general, courtiers, desirers of honour and preferment." (From Zadkiel's 1852 abridgment, An Introduction to Astrology, Chapter VIII, 'Of the Sun, His General and Particular Significations' — a public-domain modernized-spelling reprint tradition of Lilly's material, not a claim that these are Lilly's exact 1647 words; confidence: ○.)

**The record — William Lilly (1647):** The chapter already quoted above for the Sun's ranks-and-titles significations continues into character — Lilly's own two faces of the 'Solar man,' offered as a historical reading, not a claim on anyone born under the Sun:

“Then the Solar man is Arrogant and Proud, disdaining all men, cracking of his Pedigree, he is Pur-blind in Sight and Judgment, restless, troublesome, domineering, a mere vapour, expensive, foolish, endued with no gravity in words, or soberness in Actions, a Spend-thrift, wasting his Patrimony, and hanging on other men's charity, yet thinks all men are bound to him, because a Gentleman born.” Of his supposed corporature and well-dignified manners: “Usually the Sun presents a man of a good, large and strong Corporature, a yellow, saffron Complexion, a round, large Forehead; goggle Eyes or large, sharp and piercing; a Body strong and well composed, not so beautiful as lovely, full of heat, their hair yellowish, and therefore quickly bald… in conditions they are very bountiful, honest, sincere, well-minded, of great and large Heart, High-minded, of healthful Constitution, very humane, yet sufficiently Spirited, not Loquacious.” (Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I, 'Of the Sun, His General and Particular Significations.')
sections.Jyotiṣa (Bṛhat Jātaka):
**In the text:** Chapter II of the Bṛhat Jātaka ("Definitions and Elementary Planetary Principles") gives the Sun a place among the Kālapuruṣa correspondences — the scheme that maps the nine grahas onto the body and rank of a cosmic "Time-Person": the Sun and Moon are its kings, and the Sun and Moon together are called the "kings" of the planetary hierarchy, with Mars as general, Mercury as first prince, Jupiter and Venus as counsellors, and Saturn as servant. The Sun is said to be strong in bones and to preside over copper colour. (Paraphrase of Chapter II, stanza-level material, via the chestofbooks.com mirror of the Chidambaram Iyer 1885 translation; confidence: ○ — search-triangulated this session, not independently re-fetched from the primary page.)

**What this lens reads:** In tropical astrology the Sun anchors the whole zodiac (0° Aries is defined by the Sun's position at the equinox); in Jyotiṣa the Sun is one king among grahas measured against the fixed stars, roughly 24° behind its tropical degree today. Same star, two honest coordinate systems — the gap between them is the thing worth noticing, not a discrepancy to resolve.

**The record — Varāhamihira, tr. Iyer (1885):** Chapter II (‘Definitions and Elementary Principles — Planetary’), stanza 1: ‘To the Kalapurusha, the Sun is the soul… Of the planets the Sun and Moon are kings, Mars is General, Mercury is the first prince, Jupiter and Venus are counsellors and Saturn is servant.’ Stanzas 4–5 give his colour and rulership: ‘The Sun is of a red and dark-brown color… The Sun presides over copper color… The Sun is Agni [the fire-god]… The Sun presides over east.’ Stanza 7 places him by caste and temperament: ‘Mars and the Sun are Kshatriyas… The Moon, the Sun and Jupiter are of Satwaguna (good temper).’ Stanza 8 gives his physical description: ‘The Sun has somewhat yellow eyes, is of the height of the length of the two arms stretched out, of bilious nature and with very little hair on his head.’ Stanza 11: the Sun is strong ‘in bones.’ Chapter I stanza 13’s exaltation table gives Aries, 10th degree, as his sign of Uccha (exaltation), with Libra as Neecha (depression); stanza 14 names Leo as his Moolatrikona house. (Bṛhat Jātaka, tr. N. Chidambaram Iyer, 1885, Chapter II stanzas 1, 4–5, 7–8, 11; Chapter I stanzas 13–14.)
sections.Alan Leo:
**Interpretation:** The Sun represents the immortal Individuality, the divine spark within. It shows what we are becoming through evolution, our essential spiritual nature. In the horoscope, a strong Sun indicates one who can express their true self with power and authority. The Sun is the life-giver, and its position shows where we must shine.

**Keywords:** Individuality

**The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Nativity, 1903):** The Sun, we are taught by those who are seeking the Path of Wisdom, is the body of God, the Logos of this solar system, through which He gives His Love, Light and Life. In astrologic study the Sun gives to every living organism its Prāna, or life and heat, each individual specialising his own store from the cosmic Prāna. Every living thing is plunged into a great ocean of life — God's life; and every organism, whether great or small, appropriates to itself some of this universal life which is ever flowing from the Sun, the vehicle through which the Solar Logos is manifesting. The Sun, giving life, light and heat to the world, stands in each nativity as the symbol of vitality and activity, mind and intellect, love and feeling. In one word it represents the centre of each separate individual character as the sum total of himself, by absorbing into himself as much of the influence of the solar rays and the planetary vibrations as possible during his previous physical manifestations.
sections.Planetary Myths:
**Greco-Roman:** Helios, a Titan, drove a four-horse chariot across the sky each day, lighting the world from dawn to dusk. By the Hellenistic period the Olympian Apollo — god of prophecy, music, and healing — had absorbed most of Helios's solar identity in cult and art, though the two were never formally merged in myth. Sources: Wikipedia, "Selene" (cross-referenced) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selene; Greek Names, "Greek names of the planets" — https://www.greek-names.info/greek-names-of-the-planets/ (confidence: ○ — search-triangulated, direct Wikipedia fetch blocked this session).

**Vedic (graha):** Sūrya is the graha of soul, vitality, and self-worth — Jyotiṣa treats him as king among the nine grahas and the significator (kāraka) of ego, father, and life-force. He rides a seven-horse chariot driven by Aruṇa, the horses named for the seven Vedic poetic meters (chandas); his arrival is heralded by the dawn-goddess Uṣas. The Ṛgveda's Gāyatrī mantra (3.62.10) is addressed to Sūrya-as-Savitṛ. As taught in Jyotiṣa, summarized — see Wikipedia, "Surya" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surya; Budaya Bali, "God Surya and the 7 Horses" — https://budayabali.com/god-surya-and-the-7-horses-the-timekeeper-energy-controller-and-guardian-of-cosmic-balance (confidence: ○).

**Babylonian/Mesopotamian:** Shamash (Sumerian Utu) was sun-god and god of justice — riding his chariot by day, he was believed to see every human act and so judge right from wrong; Hammurabi's law code claims Shamash as its source. With Sin (Moon) and Ishtar (Venus) he formed an astral triad governing the Babylonian omen-sky, the oldest documented layer beneath the later Greco-Roman planet names. Sources: World History Encyclopedia, "Utu-Shamash" — https://www.worldhistory.org/Utu-Shamash/; Britannica, "Shamash" — https://www.britannica.com/topic/Shamash (confidence: ✔ — corroborated across independent reference sources).

**What the lens reads:** Three unrelated cultures pointed at the same bright disk and each built a different story: a chariot-driving Titan who became a healer-god, a soul-significator riding meters-of-poetry horses, a judge who sees every human act. None of this is a claim that the Sun causes anything — it is a record of how differently situated humans, looking at the same sky, made sense together. The disagreement between the three readings IS the content.
sections.Dignities & Rulerships (traditional tabl:
**Dignities table:** Domicile: Leo · Exaltation: Aries (19°) · Detriment: Aquarius · Fall: Libra

**What dignity means:** [William Lilly, Christian Astrology, 1647; general doctrine quoted via Zadkiel's 1852 abridgment] Essential dignity is placement-strength, and Lilly scores it: domicile +5, exaltation +4, triplicity +3, term +2, face +1; detriment −5, fall −4; a planet with no dignity at all is 'peregrine' — a wanderer. In its own house a planet "represents a man in such a condition as that he is lord of his own house, estate, and fortune"; exalted, "a person of haughty condition, arrogant, assuming more to himself than his due" — dignity is strength, not niceness. So the Sun in Leo commands from home ground; exalted at 19° Aries it blazes at its most assertive (and most self-important); in Aquarius (detriment) and Libra (fall) the royal claim is a guest in signs that answer to Saturn. (Scoring corroborated across multiple independent sources this session; the two quoted phrases rest on Zadkiel's public-domain abridgment of Lilly; confidence: medium.)

**Canonical:** Modern astrology keeps the Sun's rulership of Leo unchanged — no discovered planet ever claimed it. The exaltation-in-Aries / fall-in-Libra axis is usually read psychologically now: identity most radiant where it initiates, most diffuse where it defers.

**The record — Raphael (A Manual of Astrology, 1828):** [Raphael, A Manual of Astrology, 1828] “The Sun is considered as temperately hot and dry, of his own nature scarcely good or evil, but a most powerful source of ill fortune where afflicted by the other planets, and placed in his debilities, or signs contrary to his nature; as on the contrary, when strongly aspected or placed … in signs of dignity … he is the source of much prosperity.” Of the native “when principal significator”: “a large bony athletic strong body, broad high forehead, light sandy curling hair, quick piercing eye, and well made person … If well dignified or favourably aspected, the disposition is noble, magnanimous, proud and lofty, but humane; a faithful friend, and a generous enemy, scorning to use advantages which may be given him over his opponents … If ill dignified, and ill aspected, the native is both proud and mean, arrogant and submissive, a tyrant, and yet a sycophant, empty, vain, a great talker, restless, vain boasting, uncharitable, despotical, unfeeling.” (Verbatim from the 1828 djvu text this session, spelling as printed; confidence: high.)

**The record — Sepharial (Astrology: How to Make and Read Your Own Horoscope, 1920):** [Sepharial, Astrology: How to Make and Read Your Own Horoscope, 1920] “The Sun renders its subjects magnanimous, noble, proud, despising all mean and sordid actions; loyal, truthful, and fearless. It produces honours and the favour of dignitaries, and renders the subject fortunate in the control of his affairs. In the body it controls the vital principle.” Nearly a century after Raphael, the same vocabulary of nobility and honour survives almost unchanged — worth noting as continuity, not claimed as this compiler's judgment. (Verbatim from the Project Gutenberg edition this session; confidence: high.)

sections.Canonical:
**Story:** The Moon is your emotional body — how you feel, what you need, and where you seek comfort. It governs your instinctual responses and your relationship to home, nurturing, and memory.

**Light:** Emotional intelligence, receptivity, nurturing, intuition, responsiveness.

**Shadow:** Moodiness, dependency, emotional overwhelm, clinging to the past.

**Archetype:** The Mother — the container that holds and nourishes life.
sections.Ptolemy (Tetrabiblos):
**Interpretation:** The Moon principally generates moisture; her proximity to the earth renders her highly capable of exciting damp vapours, and of thus operating sensibly upon animal bodies by relaxation and putrefaction. She has, however, also a moderate share in the production of heat, in consequence of the illumination she receives from the Sun.

**Light:** The Moon is considered benefic for the same reasons as Jupiter and Venus. She is feminine, nocturnal, and governs the rhythms of change through her phases.

**Shadow:** Her proximity to the earth causes her to operate sensibly upon animal bodies by relaxation and putrefaction.

**The record — Ptolemy, tr. Ashmand (1822):** *Book I, Ch. IV–VII, on the Moon's temperament and sect (excerpted, fetched from sacred-texts.com; … marks elisions):*

> The Moon principally generates moisture; her proximity to the earth renders her highly capable of exciting damp vapours, and of thus operating sensibly upon animal bodies by relaxation and putrefaction. She has, however, also a moderate share in the production of heat, in consequence of the illumination she receives from the Sun. … And the Moon also is so considered [benefic, a causer of good, for the same reasons as Jupiter and Venus]. … The Moon and Venus are therefore said to be feminine, since their qualities are principally moist. … [T]he Moon and Venus are esteemed to be nocturnal.
sections.Lilly (1647):
**What Lilly reads:** This is a startlingly unflattering physical portrait next to the gentler, nurturing Moon of later astrology (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical) — swelling, watery-eyed, boar-toothed. Lilly's Moon-native description reads more like a period medical case-note on phlegmatic humoral excess than a psychological temperament sketch; the vividness is the point of reading him at all.

**Lilly's own words:** A Moon-dominant person appears "in a great and full body, soft and phlegmatic, of colour like a black obscure cloud, having a swelling countenance, with eyes red and full of water, a bald head, and teeth like a wilde boar." (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I; confidence: ○ — corroborated across secondary reproductions this session.)

**The record — William Lilly (1647):** The Moon chapter opens with her ancient names before turning to manners — Lilly's own reading of the Moon's changeable temper, well- and ill-placed:

“The Moon we find called by the Ancients, Lucina, Cynthia, Diana, Phoebe, Latona, Noctiluca, Proserpina; she is the nearest to the Earth of all the Planets… She is a Feminine, Nocturnal Planet, Cold, Moist and Phlegmatic.” Well placed: “She signifieth one of composed Manners, a soft, tender creature, a Lover of all honest and ingenious Sciences, a Searcher of and Delighter in Novelties, naturally prone to flit and shift her Habitation, unsteadfast, wholly caring for the present Times, Timorous, Prodigal, and easily Frighted, however loving Peace, and to live free from the cares of this Life.” Ill placed: “A mere Vagabond, idle Person, hating Labour, a Drunkard, a Sot, one of no Spirit or Forecast, delighting to live beggarly and carelessly, one content in no condition of Life, either good or ill.” (Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I, 'Of the Moon, Her Properties and Significations.')
sections.Jyotiṣa (Bṛhat Jātaka):
**In the text:** Chapter II describes the Moon-native's body as "well rounded," full of wind and phlegm, intelligent, and of sweet speech; white is the colour Candra presides over. In the Kālapuruṣa scheme the Moon is mind (manas) and, with the Sun, one of the two "kings" among the grahas. (Paraphrase with short quoted phrases from Chapter II via the chestofbooks.com mirror of the 1885 Chidambaram Iyer translation; confidence: ○.)

**What this lens reads:** Where the tropical Western literature (see grammars/western-astrology-canonical, grammars/alan-leo) reads the Moon as feeling and instinct, this text reads it as manas — mind itself, the faculty that receives and processes, not merely emotion. The Sanskrit vocabulary carves the psyche differently than the Greek-derived one does; that's a real difference in what a chart is claimed to show, not just a translation gap.

**The record — Varāhamihira, tr. Iyer (1885):** Chapter II, stanza 1: ‘the Moon is the mind [manas].’ Stanzas 4–5: ‘the Moon is white… The Moon presides over white color… the Moon is Varuna… the Moon [presides over] north-west.’ Stanza 7: ‘the Moon is a Vysya [merchant caste]… The Moon, the Sun and Jupiter are of Satwaguna (good temper).’ Stanza 8 gives her body: ‘The Moon has a thin and a round body, is of an exceedingly windy and phlegmatic nature, is learned and has a soft voice and beautiful eyes.’ Stanza 11: strong ‘in blood.’ Stanza 6 lists her among the female planets: ‘the Moon and Venus are female planets.’ Chapter I stanza 13’s table gives Taurus, 3rd degree, as her Uccha (exaltation), with Scorpio as Neecha (depression); stanza 14 names Taurus also as her Moolatrikona house; Chapter I stanza 6 names her lord of Kataka (Cancer), her only house. (Bṛhat Jātaka, tr. Iyer 1885, Chapter II stanzas 1, 4–8, 11; Chapter I stanzas 6, 13–14.)
sections.Alan Leo:
**Interpretation:** The Moon represents the Personality, the sum of past experiences carried into this life. It shows our habits, instincts, and automatic responses—what we have been. The Moon governs the physical body, the public, women, and all matters of common everyday life. Its position shows our receptive, feeling nature.

**Keywords:** Personality

**The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Nativity, 1903):** The Moon acts as the vehicle, or link of communication between the Sun and each living thing. In Astrology the Moon is the representation of the Personality, the portion of the individual that is manifested during the one life period, and as such the Moon's position and aspects become the most important when judging a nativity. If the Moon has no aspect whatever with the Sun, or is in much affliction with this luminary, then the life forces do not flow evenly, the mentality is not so sharp and clear, and the feelings are apt to be distorted; but the principal effect of the affliction is to hinder the flow of the life-current and thus affect the general health. … The permanent and vital conditions of each life are denoted by the Sun, and the fleeting and impermanent personal conditions are indicated by the Moon, this latter luminary thus representing the focussing point of a nativity.
sections.Planetary Myths:
**Greco-Roman:** Selene, a Titan daughter of Hyperion and Theia, drove her own moon-chariot nightly across the sky, sister to the sun-god Helios; the Romans called her Luna, who had a temple on Rome's Aventine Hill. In post-classical practice Selene/Luna increasingly blended with Artemis/Diana, goddess of the hunt and wilderness, even though the two began as separate figures — one purely a sky-orb goddess, the other a broader nature deity. Sources: Wikipedia, "Selene" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selene; Theoi Project, "Selene" — https://www.theoi.com/Titan/Selene.html (confidence: ○).

**Vedic (graha):** Chandra (also called Soma, "the bright drop") governs the mind (manas) in Jyotiṣa — a fast-moving, changeable graha tied to emotion, memory, and the 27 nakṣatras, mythologized as his 27 wives, daughters of Daksha. Chandra's favoritism toward Rohiṇī drew Daksha's curse of a wasting sickness, later softened into the Moon's waxing-and-waning cycle — the tradition's own explanation for lunar phases. Whether "Soma" originally meant the Moon versus the ritual drink varies by textual layer, sources note. As taught in Jyotiṣa, summarized — Wikipedia, "Chandra" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra; Dharma Station, "The Myth of Chandra and His 27 Wives" — https://www.dharmastation.ca/post/the-myth-of-chandra-and-his-27-wives (confidence: ○).

**Babylonian/Mesopotamian:** Nanna (Akkadian Sin), one of Mesopotamia's oldest attested gods (from c. 3500 BCE), was worshipped as moon-god and god of wisdom at his great ziggurat in Ur; during the Ur III period he was additionally cast as judge of the dead. Son of Enlil and Ninlil, he was symbolized by the crescent moon. Source: World History Encyclopedia, "Nanna" — https://www.worldhistory.org/Nanna/ (confidence: ○ — single strong tertiary source, content consistent with other reference summaries).

**What the lens reads:** A Titan sister on a nightly chariot ride, a wisdom-god whose crescent watches from a ziggurat in Ur, a changeable mind-graha with 27 star-brides — three cultures, one visibly-changing light in the night sky. Nobody in this grammar is claiming the Moon governs mood; the claim is narrower and more honest: humans across millennia independently reached for story to hold what they could plainly see changing shape above them.
sections.Dignities & Rulerships (traditional tabl:
**Dignities table:** Domicile: Cancer · Exaltation: Taurus (3°) · Detriment: Capricorn · Fall: Scorpio

**What dignity means:** [William Lilly, Christian Astrology, 1647] By Lilly's scoring (domicile +5, exaltation +4; detriment −5, fall −4, with triplicity, term, and face as the lesser dignities of +3/+2/+1) the Moon is strongest at home in Cancer, where her tides are her own, and exalted at 3° Taurus — the zodiac's most changeable body given its steadiest ground. In Capricorn (detriment) her nurture is rationed by rule; in Scorpio (fall) her instinct runs to extremes. (Placements: high confidence, heavily cross-corroborated; the reading is this compiler's gloss on the shared table, not Lilly's wording.)

**Canonical:** Modern astrology keeps the Moon's rulership of Cancer unchanged. The exaltation at 3° Taurus is among the oldest attested of all the degrees — Dorotheus's Carmen already carries it — and is usually read now as feeling finding safety in the body and the ordinary.

**The record — Raphael (A Manual of Astrology, 1828):** [Raphael, A Manual of Astrology, 1828] “The Moon, the companion of the earth, and chief source of our evening light, is a cold, moist, watery, phlegmatic planet, variable to an extreme … and partaking of good or evil, as she is aspected by good or evil stars. When angular and unafflicted in a nativity, she is the promissory pledge of great success in life, and continual good fortune … Her conjunction, semisextile, sextile, or trine, to Jupiter, is exceedingly fortunate.” Her enemies are given as Saturn and the Sun, her other aspects friendly. (Verbatim from the 1828 djvu text this session; confidence: high.)

**The record — Sepharial (Astrology: How to Make and Read Your Own Horoscope, 1920):** [Sepharial, Astrology: How to Make and Read Your Own Horoscope, 1920] “The Moon gives gracefulness of manner and suavity of speech, softness and adaptability of nature, variableness, love of change, romance, and adventure; disposed to exploration and voyaging. In the body it corresponds to the glandular system, and its diseases are those incidental to the lymphatic glands and vascular tissue.” (Verbatim from the Project Gutenberg edition this session; confidence: high.)

sections.Canonical:
**Story:** Mercury is the mind in motion — how you think, communicate, and make sense of the world. It governs language, learning, commerce, and the bridges between things.

**Light:** Articulate, curious, adaptable, quick-witted, perceptive.

**Shadow:** Overthinking, trickery, scattered attention, nervousness.

**Archetype:** The Messenger — the one who carries meaning between worlds.
sections.Ptolemy (Tetrabiblos):
**Interpretation:** Mercury sometimes produces dryness, and at other times moisture, and each with equal vigour. His faculty of absorbing moisture and creating dryness proceeds from his situation with regard to the Sun, from which he is at no time far distant in longitude; and, on the other hand, he produces moisture, because he borders upon the Moon's sphere.

**Light:** Mercury is common to both genders, and common in influence—diurnal when matutine, nocturnal when vespertine. His rapid motion produces rapid changes.

**Shadow:** Being excited by the velocity of his motion with the Sun, he consequently operates rapid changes tending to produce alternately either quality.

**The record — Ptolemy, tr. Ashmand (1822):** *Book I, Ch. IV–VII, on Mercury's temperament and sect (excerpted, fetched from sacred-texts.com; … marks elisions):*

> Mercury sometimes produces dryness, and at other times moisture, and each with equal vigour. His faculty of absorbing moisture and creating dryness proceeds from his situation with regard to the Sun, from which he is at no time far distant in longitude; and, on the other hand, he produces moisture, because he borders upon the Moon's sphere, which is nearest to the earth; and, being thus excited by the velocity of his motion with the Sun, he consequently operates rapid changes tending to produce alternately either quality. … The Sun and Mercury are deemed of common influence, and productive either of good or evil in unison with whatever planets they may be connected with. … Mercury is common to both genders, because at certain times he produces dryness, and at others moisture, and performs each in an equal ratio. … Mercury, common; since in his matutine position he is diurnal, but nocturnal when vespertine.
sections.Lilly (1647):
**What Lilly reads:** 'Author of subtilty, tricks, devices, perjury' is a considerably darker Mercury than the Hellenistic 'common, convertible' planet (grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand) or the Vedic Budha's speech-and-cleverness portfolio (grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka) — Lilly's 17th-century English Mercury leans hard toward the trickster and the liar, a moralizing gloss the other two traditions' texts don't emphasize as strongly.

**Lilly's own words:** Mercury "rules the animal spirit: he is author of subtilty, tricks, devices, perjury, &c." — his nature convertible, taking on the quality of whatever planet he associates with, fittingly for a planet Lilly elsewhere treats as neither wholly masculine nor feminine, neither fully fortunate nor unfortunate. (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I; confidence: ○.)

**The record — William Lilly (1647):** Lilly's Mercury opens with the planet's classical names and its odd genderlessness, then gives its own well- and ill-dignified pair, in his own moralizing register:

“It is called Hermes, Stilbon, Cyllenius, Archas. **Babylonian/Mesopotamian:** Inanna (Akkadian Ishtar), among the oldest deities for whom written evidence survives, combined love, sex, and fertility with war and political power — an unusual pairing for a single figure. Her eight-pointed star marked her identification with Venus in both its "Morning Star" (warrior) and "Evening Star" (beauty) aspects; her myth of descending to the underworld and returning has been read as a mirror of Venus's own disappearance and reappearance in the sky. **What the lens reads:** Love-goddess and war-goddess, teacher of demons with power to revive the dead, a beauty born from severed divinity in sea-foam — the throughline across three traditions is a bright, twin-aspected planet (morning star and evening star are literally the same body) mapped onto love, value, and attraction. The lens reads a real astronomical phenomenon — Venus's two appearances — through three unrelated symbol systems; none of the three is 'the' correct reading.

But, owing to the spheres of Mars and the Sun, which lie beneath him, his warmth is predominant: and hence he produces fertilizing breezes.

**Light:** Jupiter is considered by the ancients as benefic, or causer of good, because heat and moisture are predominant in him. He produces fertilizing breezes and promotes growth.

Rome's Jupiter inherited Zeus's role as king of the gods and god of sky, law, and order. **Babylonian/Mesopotamian:** Marduk began as a minor agricultural god of Babylon before Hammurabi's reign (c. 1792 BCE) elevated him to supreme sky-god and king of the pantheon. The Enūma Eliš epic tells how he defeated the primordial sea-goddess Tiamat and built the heavens and earth from her body — the mythic charter for Babylon's claim to cosmic and political centrality. Later astral texts equate him with the planet Jupiter. Sources: World History Encyclopedia, "Enuma Elish"; EBSCO Research Starters, "Marduk" — https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/religion-and-philosophy/marduk (confidence: ✔ for the Enuma Elish narrative, ○ for the specific Jupiter equation's dating).

**What the lens reads:** A thunder-king who overthrew his own father, a wisdom-teacher whose bowstring is cosmic order itself, a city-god who slew chaos and built the world from its corpse — three cultures independently cast their largest visible wandering star as the "biggest" kind of god: king, teacher, world-orderer. The size and brightness of Jupiter in the sky maps onto "bigness" of role across traditions that never spoke to each other.

sections.Ptolemy (Tetrabiblos):
**Interpretation:** Saturn produces cold and dryness, for he is most remote both from the Sun's heat and from the earth's vapours. But he is more effective in the production of cold than of dryness. Saturn is esteemed malefic, or causer of evil, from his excess of cold. The coldness of Saturn is allotted to the day, to counterbalance its heat.

**Light:** When moderated by combination with day, Saturn produces a favourable temperament. His influence brings structure, time, and the wisdom of age and distance.

**Shadow:** Malefic, causer of evil from excess of cold. Saturn and Mars are esteemed of a contrary nature to the benefics, noxious in their influence.

**The record — Ptolemy, tr. Ashmand (1822):** *Book I, Ch. IV–VII, on Saturn's temperament and sect (excerpted, fetched from sacred-texts.com; … marks elisions):*

> Saturn produces cold and dryness, for he is most remote both from the Sun's heat and from the earth's vapours. But he is more effective in the production of cold than of dryness. … Saturn and Mars are esteemed of a contrary nature, and malefic, or causers of evil: the first from his excess of cold, the other from his excess of dryness. … The Sun, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are called masculine. … Of the other two planets, Saturn and Mars, which are noxious, one is considered to be diurnal, and the other nocturnal … Hence the coldness of Saturn is allotted to the day, to counterbalance its heat; and the dryness of Mars to the night, to counterbalance its moisture. **Greco-Roman:** Kronos, youngest Titan, castrated his father Uranus and later swallowed his own children on hearing a prophecy he would be overthrown by one of them; Zeus, hidden by Rhea, survived to force his siblings back out and depose him. Beneath the horror-myth, Kronos was likely an older harvest-god — his festival, the Kronia, was a harvest celebration echoed by Rome's Saturnalia. Sources: Wikipedia, "Cronus" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronus; Theoi Project, "Cronus" — https://www.theoi.com/Titan/TitanKronos.html (confidence: ✔).

**Vedic (graha):** Shani, son of Sūrya (the Sun) and his wife's shadow-double Chhāyā, is Jyotiṣa's grim significator of karma, justice, and time's slow reckoning — appointed, in later myth, to oversee everyone's karmic account without exception. His birth story says his first infant glance caused a solar eclipse, and that Sūrya himself could not bear to look at his dark-complexioned son directly. As taught in Jyotiṣa, summarized — Wikipedia, "Shani" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shani; Exotic India, "All About Shani Dev" — https://www.exoticindiaart.com/article/all-about-shani-dev/ (confidence: ○).

**Babylonian/Mesopotamian:** Saturn's Mesopotamian layer is the least settled of the seven: 1st-millennium astral texts (e.g. MUL.APIN) equate Saturn with Ninurta, a farmer-and-war god, but earlier tradition (under the variant name Ninib) sometimes cast the same figure as a solar deity instead — a real ambiguity in the sources, not a settled one-to-one mapping. What's firmer: Ninurta's harvest-god role parallels Kronos's, plausibly why the Greek-to-Babylonian chain (Kronos = Saturn = Ninurta) held. Sources: Ancient Mesopotamia, "Ninurta" — https://ancientmesopotamia.org/ideology/ninurta; Wikipedia, "Ninurta" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninurta (confidence: ◆ contested — flagged as such in the sources themselves, not just by us).

**What the lens reads:** A child-devouring Titan who was secretly a harvest-god, a karma-accountant whose own father couldn't bear to look at him, a Mesopotamian farmer-god whose "Saturn" identity even ancient scribes weren't fully consistent about — Saturn is the one planet where every tradition, including the oldest layer, treats the assignment as difficult and heavy. That the ancients themselves disagreed about which god belongs here is worth sitting with, not smoothing over.

sections.Alan Leo:

The five physical senses find their outlet through this ascendant, and much depends upon the nature of the sign rising and any planets in the ascendant, if such there are, as regards the expression of the Ego in the physical world. It belongs to the triangle of the seventh and third houses, and has a great deal in common with both of these. By secondary influence it stands to the seventh house as the fifth stands to the first; that is, it is the fifth house of the marriage partner, and therefore has to be taken into account when considering questions concerning children and the other affairs of the fifth house. Taken by itself, free from affliction, it may be considered a benefic house, as its natural tendency seems to be towards good fortune, pleasure, happiness and prosperity; and benefics in this house or planets well aspected will benefit the native, socially or otherwise, and lift him up in the world, according to the nature of the planet. It has a great deal of sympathy also with the tenth house; and is often found containing strong or fortunate planets in the horoscopes of persons who are prominent in politics, in municipal affairs, or who in business matters are concerned with the many rather than the few, through factories, companies, associations, stores, societies, etc.

**Interpretation:** The house of seclusion, karma, and self-undoing. It governs hospitals, prisons, hidden enemies, and the unconscious. This house shows our hidden strengths and weaknesses, and the soul's need for retreat.

**Keywords:** Karma

**The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Nativity, 1903):** The twelfth house is generally supposed to be the house of sorrow, enemies, imprisonment and misfortune. This is probably owing to its being one of the houses belonging to the psychic trinity; and, as the cadent houses of that triangle, it is the least fortunate of the three. … The Cardinal houses or 'Angles' represent the physical body, and all that is expressed by action in the outer or external world; they are quick, acute, active, energetic, open. … The Succedent houses are less physical and material in their nature, being more in sympathy with the feelings and emotions. … The Cadent houses are the least expressed of any signs; they govern the mind and thought more than emotion or action, and are more closely related to the limbs of the body than the other signs. … The third, sixth, ninth and twelfth signs in the order of the signs are common or mutable signs and in the order of the twelve houses are the 'cadent' houses; these are 'unfortunate,' owing to their latency or lack of practical external expression.
